newsitem.title: GERMANY: Saxony state seeks aid framework from EU.
newsitem.headline: Saxony state seeks aid framework from EU.

text.p: Saxony state in the former communist east Germany on Friday called on the European Commission to grant the region special status for receiving state aid until the year 2005.

Kurt Biedenkopf, Saxony premiere, in a letter to members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats that was obtained by the daily Leipziger Volkszeitung, said Brussels needed to agree on a legal framework that would regulate state aid for the struggling east Germany along the lines of German law.
Excerpts from the letter were released ahead of publication in the newspaper on Saturday.
Bonn and Brussels have been fighting over Saxony's insistence on paying subsidies to car maker Volkswagen AG, even after the European Commission had rejected the aid.
The row has grown quiet recently, but the two sides are still pursuing the matter in the European Court in the event that a compromise is not reached.

Biedenkopf stated that an agreement on aid until 2005 would be in line with German legislation that states that east Germany at that time would stop receiving certain forms of compensation from west German states.
"If there were an agreement along these lines, then the legal disputes in the European Court could also be resolved," Biedenkopf wrote.

The German government and the European Commission have been embroiled in a dispute after Saxony state paid 91 million marks ($59.7 million) in aid for two VW plants in Mosel and Chemnitz, to create 23,000 jobs after the Commission ruled against the aid.

Biedenkopf refused to repay the aid, but a face- saving compromise was eventually found. Instead of paying back the cash, Bonn will withhold a similar amount of assistance until Germany and the Commission come up with a lasting solution.

The Saxony premiere rejected earlier charges by European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert that the state's payment of aid to VW was in violation of EU law and said the Commission had failed to properly study this specific case.
"We also doubt that Commissioner Van Miert really knows the specifics of this case," Biedenkopf wrote. ($ = 1.524 German Marks)
